Graph-based spectral methods can scale to large networks by avoiding a full eigendecomposition of the graph Laplacian or affinity matrix. Instead of computing all eigenvectors, they typically use sparse graph representations, iterative solvers, and low-rank or approximate techniques such as Lanczos/Arnoldi methods, Nyström-style approximations, or other randomized/partial spectral methods to obtain only the few leading components needed for embedding or clustering. This makes them much more practical on large, sparse networks than exact spectral decomposition.

Compared with PCA, the key difference is that PCA is usually based on a covariance matrix and can often be computed efficiently with randomized or incremental SVD, but it is fundamentally a linear method on vector data rather than a graph method. Compared with IsoMap, spectral graph methods are generally more scalable because IsoMap requires building a neighborhood graph and then computing shortest-path geodesic distances followed by an eigendecomposition of the resulting distance/kernel matrix, which becomes expensive in both time and memory as the network grows. In short, graph spectral methods keep the graph structure but replace exact eigendecomposition with sparse/approximate spectral computations, making them more scalable than IsoMap and often more suitable for very large networks.
